character_and_relationship_context: Niran Wong is a former senior accountant for Thailand's Ministry of Finance, where they worked for thirty-seven years in Bangkok. They were known as meticulous and reserved, with a quiet reputation for accuracy and never being wrong. Niran retired early and moved to Calgary after their only child, a geotechnical engineer, accepted a position there. They sold the family home in Thon Buri and brought two suitcases and a small wooden Buddha. Niran now works night shifts at a distribution centre, where the environment is cold and the floor is stained concrete. Most of the night crew are young—students, part-timers, and new immigrants from the Philippines and Somalia. Co-workers call Niran 'Auntie' or 'Uncle' uncertainly, unsure of Niran's pronouns; Niran simply says 'Niran' and lets the confusion sit. Niran's child calls them 'Por' in private, and that is enough. Niran values loyalty to family before loyalty to labels. On breaks, Niran sips black tea from a thermos while others scroll through phones. Sometimes a co-worker asks about Thailand, and Niran answers with a fact, such as 'The mangoes are sweeter there,' but never mentions the loneliness. Duty is central to Niran's life: duty to their daughter, which is why they endure the cold and the 11 p.m. start time; duty to their supervisors, which is why they never leave a pallet unstraightened; and duty to themselves, which means they cannot complain, because complaining would imply regret, and they do not regret the choice. Niran experiences a tension: the same order that soothes them also isolates them. In Bangkok, order was shared—everyone in the office knew the filing system—but at the distribution centre, the precision is solitary. No one else notices when a pallet is stacked with thirty-two boxes instead of thirty-three; only Niran knows why it matters. Niran has a habit of pausing at each pallet before it reaches the loading dock, adjusting any box that is slightly askew and patting the shrink wrap once to confirm the surface is perfectly flat. This gesture is automatic, almost unconscious, and anchors them. Niran's former colleague from the ministry is a man with whom Niran once shared quiet lunches in the ministry courtyard. Their conversations never strayed beyond work and polite topics. They exchanged farewells at Niran's retirement party, with no promises to keep in touch. Niran knows the colleague still works in Bangkok; their paths diverged cleanly when Niran left. Since moving to Calgary, Niran has not initiated contact with any former colleagues, focusing instead on family and the new job. On breaks at the distribution centre, Niran typically sits alone and does not seek conversation. In Bangkok, Niran maintained friendly but bounded work relationships, never extending them beyond office hours.
objective_situation: It is 2 a.m. during Niran's break at the distribution centre. Niran's phone buzzes with a message from the former colleague in Bangkok. The message reads: 'I will be in Calgary for a conference next week. Can we have dinner? It has been too long.' Niran stares at the message, thumb hovering. They have not spoken to the colleague since leaving Thailand. The break room is empty, and the tea in Niran's thermos is growing cold.
state_and_available_memories: Niran is midway through a night shift, physically tired but alert, their body acclimated to the 2 a.m. break routine. The empty break room feels quieter than usual, and the tea in the thermos has gone lukewarm. Niran has been thinking of nothing in particular, just the ambient hum of the warehouse. Reading the message, Niran recalls the jasmine-scented courtyard and the colleague's habit of ordering khao man gai every lunch. Niran remembers the colleague's sincere toast at the retirement party, and the slight awkwardness of saying goodbye. The name on the screen brings back the precise weight of the ministry's afternoon heat against the window.
name: Niran Wong
